title: Sensor line steerco

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Alright, let's get going, thanks everyone.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Usual agenda, program status, budget, timeline risk, engineering readiness, then decisions.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Sun, want to open?

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: Sure.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: Aegis is still tracking to the trade show launch window in March, that's the anchor date everything else is built around.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: We're about ten weeks out from needing production-intent units for the show floor demo, which is tighter than it sounds once you back out certification and packaging lead times.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: Engineering readiness looks good on paper, the open risk is almost entirely on the manufacturing side, specifically the enclosure tooling, which Rafael's going to walk through.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: From a program management view, I'd call us yellow overall, not red, but the enclosure risk is real enough that I want the room's full attention on it today rather than just a mention in passing.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Understood, yellow overall, enclosure risk is the headline.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Rafael, take us through it.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Thanks.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: So the enclosure is a machined and anodized aluminum housing, it's a new design for Aegis, nothing carried over from the Vantage line's molded plastic enclosure.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: We're working with the same supplier who did our Vantage tooling, Corvant Enclosures, and the short version is the anodizing step is adding more lead time than we scoped.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Original plan was six weeks for the full tool build including anodizing setup, current estimate from their last call is ten to twelve weeks once the tool is actually locked, and we're not locked yet because we're still iterating on a rib pattern for thermal dissipation.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: How many more iterations do you expect before it's locked?

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Optimistically one more, realistically two.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: The first two prototypes both showed hot spots near the radio module under sustained transmission, which is a new failure mode we didn't see on Vantage because the enclosure geometry is completely different.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: We've got a third rib pattern from thermal modeling that should resolve it, prototypes should be back from the machine shop by Thursday, so I'd know within about a week and a half whether we're locking on iteration three or need a fourth pass.

segments.speaker: spk_4
segments.text: Before you answer that, can you remind us what the actual cost is per additional prototype iteration, just so we can weigh it against the schedule risk properly?

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Sure, each prototype iteration is around eight thousand dollars for the machining and anodizing test run, plus roughly a week and a half of turnaround from the shop.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: It's not the dominant cost in this program, but three or four iterations instead of the two we budgeted does add up, and more importantly it's the schedule impact that actually worries me more than the dollar figure.

segments.speaker: spk_4
segments.text: Understood, that's helpful context, the dollar amount alone wouldn't have worried me, it's good to know the schedule risk is the bigger driver.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: If it's a fourth pass, what does that do to the ten week window Sun mentioned?

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: If we need a fourth pass, we're probably eight to ten weeks behind the original enclosure timeline instead of four to six, which would put finished enclosures arriving close to or after the show floor deadline, not comfortably ahead of it like we'd want for a demo unit that actually needs to survive being handled by strangers for three days.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: That's the scenario I wanted flagged today.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: If we're at real risk of missing the demo unit deadline, we need a contingency conversation now, not in six weeks when there's no time left to execute one.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Agreed.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: What would a contingency actually look like, Rafael, is there a faster path even if it costs more?

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: A couple of options.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: One, we could dual-source a rush tool from a second supplier in parallel, accept the extra cost, and use whichever finishes first, that's maybe three to four weeks faster but adds real budget.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Two, we could show a non-anodized, bead-blasted aluminum finish for the demo units specifically and finish the anodizing tooling properly for production units after the show, that's basically free time-wise but it's a cosmetic compromise on the demo hardware.

segments.speaker: spk_4
segments.text: What's the actual cost delta on the dual-source option, roughly?

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Rough order of magnitude, an extra forty to sixty thousand dollars for a rush tool we'd essentially throw away or repurpose for spares afterward, plus expedite fees from Corvant if we ask them to compress their own schedule in parallel.

segments.speaker: spk_4
segments.text: That's a meaningful number against the program budget we set at the top of the year, we don't have that kind of contingency sitting unused right now.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: What about the bead-blasted option, any risk beyond looking less finished?

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Minimal technical risk, the thermal and mechanical properties are identical, it's purely cosmetic, and honestly a lot of trade show attendees handle pre-production units expecting them to look a little rough anyway.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: I can live with that from a program perspective, it protects the date without blowing the budget, and it's honestly not a bad story to tell, "here's the working hardware, final finish comes with production units."

segments.speaker: spk_4
segments.text: I'd support that too, it's the more fiscally responsible path and the actual product being sold is the anodized version regardless.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Sounds like we have rough consensus, let's make that the decision, bead-blasted finish for demo units, keep the anodizing tooling on its normal timeline for production.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Rafael, can you confirm that with Corvant this week?

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Yes, I'll call them tomorrow and confirm they can turn bead-blasted units around fast enough once the rib pattern's locked, regardless of anodizing status.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Let's move to budget, Dele, where do things stand overall?

segments.speaker: spk_4
segments.text: Overall we're tracking about six percent over the original Aegis development budget, mostly driven by the enclosure iteration cost we just discussed, plus some additional bench equipment Maya's team needed for the new sensor calibration rig.

segments.speaker: spk_4
segments.text: Neither overage is alarming on its own, but together they're eating into the contingency line faster than I'd like at this stage of the program.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Is six percent something we need to formally reforecast, or is it within normal variance for a program at this stage?

segments.speaker: spk_4
segments.text: I'd call it within variance for now, but if the enclosure contingency conversation ends up costing us the dual-source option instead of the cheaper bead-blast path, that pushes us closer to ten percent, and at that point I would want a formal reforecast conversation with finance leadership rather than just noting it here.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: Good thing we're going with the cheaper path then, that keeps us out of that conversation for now.

segments.speaker: spk_4
segments.text: Agreed, and I'd like to keep it that way, so if any other risk surfaces that threatens to push another five or six points, I want to hear about it as early as Rafael flagged this one, not after the fact.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Fair, that's a good norm for this group in general, early flags over surprises.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Let's move to engineering readiness.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Maya, take us through firmware and calibration status.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Sure.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Starting with calibration, since Aegis uses a different sensor package than Vantage, we can't just reuse the existing compensation tables, we're building a new calibration model from scratch, but the underlying pipeline architecture, the soak-test methodology, the statistical approach to characterizing drift, all of that carries over directly from the work we've done on Vantage over the past year.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: I'd estimate we're saving several weeks of engineering time by not reinventing that part.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: That's good to hear, I was worried calibration would be a bigger lift given it's a new sensor.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: It's a lift, but a bounded one.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: We've characterized the new sensor against twenty units so far, on temperature and humidity, pressure characterization starts next week.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Early data looks clean, tighter tolerances than I expected actually, which is good news for the accuracy claims in the marketing materials Sun's team wants to use at the show.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: That's genuinely useful, I'll loop marketing in on preliminary numbers once you're comfortable sharing them, even informally.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: I'd say give it two more weeks before anything goes to marketing, I don't want to hand over a number I have to walk back later.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Let me actually walk through why I'm confident in the methodology, since I know not everyone in this room lives in calibration curves day to day.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: The core idea is we're not just checking that a sensor reads correctly at room temperature, we're characterizing how its reading drifts across the full operating envelope, so we run each unit through a soak chamber cycling between minus twenty and sixty degrees Celsius at several humidity setpoints, logging continuously, and comparing against a reference instrument that's itself traceable to a calibration lab standard.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Any systematic deviation from that reference gets baked into a per-unit or per-batch compensation table that the firmware applies at runtime.

segments.speaker: spk_4
segments.text: How long does a full characterization run take per unit, since that presumably has cost implications if we're doing it at scale for production.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: For engineering characterization like what we're doing now, it's about four days per batch of twenty units, since we're cycling slowly to avoid thermal shock artifacts confusing the data.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: For production calibration, it's a much shorter targeted verification, not a full characterization, more like twenty minutes per unit on a fixture that checks against expected values at a couple of setpoints rather than the whole envelope.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: The expensive four-day process is a one-time model-building exercise, not something we repeat per unit shipped.

segments.speaker: spk_4
segments.text: That's reassuring, I was worried we'd baked a four-day-per-unit cost into the Aegis production plan somewhere.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: No, that would make the unit economics fall apart immediately, the whole point of the characterization work up front is so production calibration stays fast and cheap.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: Can you say more about what "tighter tolerances than expected" actually means in practice, is that a marketing claim we can make or an engineering nuance?

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: It's real enough to be a marketing claim, cautiously.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Across the twenty units so far, humidity readings are holding within about a quarter of a percent of reference across the full range we've tested, versus roughly half a percent on the current Vantage line with its older sensor package.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Temperature is even tighter, well within a tenth of a degree.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: I'd want the full sample size before anyone puts a specific number in a spec sheet, but directionally it's a genuine improvement, not just a rounding difference.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: That's a good story for the show, more accurate than our existing flagship line, I'll make a note to have marketing frame it carefully once you give the final go-ahead.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Understood, two weeks, then I'll sign off on specific numbers.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: This is great detail, thank you.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: Understood, I'll tell them two weeks, not sooner.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: On the firmware architecture side, we looked at whether Aegis needs its own firmware codebase or can share with Vantage.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Short answer, more shareable than we expected.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: The communication stack and the calibration pipeline architecture carry over largely unchanged, it's really the sensor driver layer and some power management specifics that need Aegis-specific code given the different hardware.

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: I can go deeper on that if useful, since I did most of the actual driver-layer investigation.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Please do, Tomas.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Before that, quickly, how did you two even validate that the shared approach was viable before sinking real time into a prototype, was there a spike or a proof of concept first?

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: Yeah, about two weeks ago Maya and I spent a day and a half doing exactly that, a spike where we tried wiring the existing Vantage calibration code against a mocked-up Aegis sensor interface, just to see how much friction there was.

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: If it had been a fight the whole way, we'd have recommended forking instead, but it came together faster than either of us expected, which is what gave us the confidence to recommend the shared approach today rather than hedge on it.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Good, I like that you tested the assumption before committing to it rather than just asserting it would work.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: That's generally how we try to approach these decisions, a day and a half of spike work is cheap insurance against weeks of committing to the wrong architecture.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Please do, Tomas.

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: Sure.

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: We prototyped a shared driver interface, basically an abstraction layer so the calibration pipeline and communication stack don't need to know which sensor package they're talking to underneath.

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: It's more upfront work than just forking the whole codebase, maybe three extra weeks of investment now, but it means every future firmware feature we build gets shared between product lines automatically instead of being implemented twice and drifting apart over time.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: And it directly avoids the headcount problem we flagged internally a few weeks ago, we don't need a fully separate firmware team for Aegis if most of the codebase is genuinely shared.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: That's a meaningful finding.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Tomas, how confident are you in the three week estimate?

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: Reasonably confident, I've already got a rough prototype of the abstraction layer working against both the Vantage and Aegis sensor packages in a lab setup, it's not zero-to-one work at this point, it's refinement and test coverage.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: I'd add, from the calibration side, that a shared architecture also means the statistical tooling I built for characterizing Vantage drift just works on Aegis data without modification, since it operates on the abstraction layer's output rather than raw sensor registers.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: That wasn't something we explicitly planned for, it just fell out of doing the abstraction properly.

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: Right, and it goes both directions, any driver-level bug fix we make for Aegis because of some quirk in the new sensor package benefits Vantage too if it turns out to be a shared code path issue rather than something sensor-specific.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: That's a nice compounding benefit.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: What does the actual test coverage plan look like for the shared layer, since that's presumably the bulk of the three weeks?

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: Roughly a week is finishing the abstraction interface itself, then two weeks is building out a proper hardware-in-the-loop test matrix that exercises both sensor packages through the same test code, so we're not writing two parallel test suites that could drift apart from each other the same way two firmware forks would have.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: And I'll be pairing with him on the calibration-specific test cases within that matrix, since I know where the tricky edge cases are, humidity extremes mostly, and temperature transitions that happen faster than the sensor's thermal mass can track.

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: That pairing's already been useful actually, Maya caught a case yesterday where the abstraction layer was rounding a humidity reading before compensation instead of after, which would have introduced a small but real error on both product lines if it had shipped.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Small thing, but exactly the kind of thing that's much easier to catch when you're building the shared test matrix deliberately instead of discovering it separately on each product line months apart.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Good, let's approve that approach then, shared codebase with the abstraction layer, rather than a fork.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Any objection from anyone?

segments.speaker: spk_4
segments.text: No objection from budget, if anything it's better for budget long-term since it avoids duplicated engineering cost on every future release.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: No objection from manufacturing, doesn't affect anything on my side either way.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: Agreed from a program view too, one codebase is easier to support post-launch regardless.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Good, that's a clean decision.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Rafael, what about certification, where does that stand?

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Certification testing is scheduled for six weeks from now, that's actually one of the tighter dependencies feeding into the March date, if the enclosure rib pattern changes again it could shift the certification test samples too, since certification needs final-geometry units, not prototypes.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: That's another reason the bead-blast decision matters, it decouples the demo unit deadline from the certification unit deadline, certification units can still wait for the properly anodized finish since they're not going on a show floor.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Right, that's actually a nice side benefit I hadn't fully connected until just now, thanks for pointing that out.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Since we're on certification, one more manufacturing-side item worth raising while everyone's here, the factory calibration station.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Maya's twenty-minute-per-unit verification process needs a physical fixture on the line, and we haven't built that yet.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Right, that's actually next on my list after the characterization work wraps.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: The fixture itself is fairly simple, a reference chamber that can hit two or three setpoints quickly and a jig that seats the unit consistently so the sensor's exposed the same way every time, but building and validating the fixture itself typically takes a few weeks once we know the final enclosure geometry, since the jig has to match the physical shape of the unit.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Which loops back to the rib pattern decision again, everything seems to trace back to that this meeting.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: It does seem to be the pinch point for almost everything today.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Maya, once the geometry is locked, how long before the calibration station itself is ready for production use?

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Call it three weeks from locked geometry to a validated station, that includes building the jig, running a pilot batch of fifty units through it to confirm repeatability, and training whoever's operating it on the line.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: I'd want that three weeks to start as close to the rib pattern lock as possible so it's not sitting at the end of the critical path on its own.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: I can make sure the jig fabrication request goes out same day as the geometry lock, no reason to wait for a formal handoff meeting.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: That would help a lot actually, even a day or two saved there adds up given how tight the rest of the timeline is.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Good, let's treat that as implicit rather than a separate action item.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Rafael, loop Maya in the moment geometry locks.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Will do.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: One more thing while we're talking production readiness, has anyone thought about data handling for the units on the factory floor during calibration?

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: We log every unit's characterization data into our internal system, and if Aegis units are also going to support the cloud connectivity feature out of the box, I want to make sure factory test data isn't accidentally reachable from a production cloud account.

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: Good catch, that's actually a real risk if the same firmware image is used for both factory testing and shipped units, the connectivity stack needs to know it's in a factory test mode and route data locally instead of to the production cloud service.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Right, and Vantage handles this today with a factory-mode flag that gets burned off during final production flashing, before the unit ever leaves the building.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: I'd want the same pattern on Aegis, and since the connectivity stack is part of the shared codebase we just approved, it should mostly just work once we wire the flag through.

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: Agreed, I'll make sure the factory-mode flag is part of the abstraction layer test matrix, not an afterthought bolted on later.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Good, glad that surfaced now rather than after units were already on a factory floor talking to the wrong server.

segments.speaker: spk_4
segments.text: That kind of thing is exactly what I worry about from a risk perspective, appreciate it being caught in a planning conversation instead of an incident report.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Good, sounds like the two decisions reinforce each other well.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Let's talk timeline holistically for a minute, Sun, given everything we've covered, does March still hold?

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: I think so, with the caveat that it's a tighter March than it was a month ago.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: The critical path now runs through certification testing in six weeks, which depends on final enclosure geometry, which depends on Rafael's rib pattern landing within the next week and a half.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: If that slips again, certification slips, and then March genuinely becomes at risk, not just tight.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: So the rib pattern decision next week and a half is really the single most important date on this whole program right now.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: That's exactly right, and I'd like us to treat it that way, meaning if Rafael needs anything from any of us to make that decision faster or with more confidence, that should be the top priority for the next ten days.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: I appreciate that, I don't think I need anything beyond what's already moving, the thermal modeling and the machine shop turnaround are both on track, but I'll flag immediately if that changes.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Good, let's make that an explicit ask then.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Sun, anything from marketing or sales we should know about?

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: Sales collateral is in progress, mostly waiting on final specs and the calibration accuracy numbers Maya mentioned.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: Marketing wants a name decision soon too, Aegis has been the internal codename this whole time, but legal's trademark search on a couple of finalist customer-facing names should come back by next week.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Out of curiosity, does the trade show booth design assume the anodized finish, or is that also flexible if we end up needing it to be?

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: It assumes anodized for the hero unit in the display case, but the units people actually pick up and handle can be the bead-blasted ones we just agreed on, that's actually pretty common practice at these shows, a pristine display unit and more durable handling units.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Good, that solves a problem I was quietly worried about, whether the booth design itself was locked to a finish we might not hit in time.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: No, we built in that flexibility a while back, mostly because trade show logistics always have some hardware uncertainty this far out, it's rarely the actual product that's fully locked at this stage.

segments.speaker: spk_4
segments.text: While you two are talking booth logistics, is there a firm budget for the booth itself, separate from the product development numbers we discussed earlier?

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: Yes, separate line entirely, booth and event costs come out of the marketing events budget, not engineering or program contingency, so that overage conversation from earlier doesn't touch it.

segments.speaker: spk_4
segments.text: Good, just wanted to make sure I wasn't missing a cost bucket somewhere.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: No, you're not, they're cleanly separated in the tracking sheet I sent around last month.

segments.speaker: spk_4
segments.text: Do we have a budget line for the name change itself, packaging reprints, website updates, that sort of thing?

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: Small one, yes, it's already in the original marketing budget, not something that would touch the engineering contingency line we discussed earlier.

segments.speaker: spk_4
segments.text: Good, just wanted to confirm those are separate pools.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Before we wrap the general discussion, let's do a quick risk roundtable, one thing each of you is watching that hasn't come up yet today.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Rafael, anything beyond the enclosure?

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Yes, actually, the sensor package itself, the one Maya's characterizing, comes from a single supplier right now, and we haven't qualified a second source.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: For Vantage that's fine, it's a mature part with plenty of supply, but Aegis's sensor is newer to the market and I'd want a backup source qualified before we're at meaningful production volume, not after a shortage hits us.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: How long does qualifying a second source typically take?

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Usually two to three months once we identify a candidate, since Maya's team has to recharacterize against the new part too, it's not just a mechanical and electrical fit check.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Right, if the second-source part has even slightly different behavior, we'd need at least a partial recharacterization, not the full four-day process necessarily, but not nothing either.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Let's add sourcing qualification to the Q1-equivalent planning list, it shouldn't be forgotten.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Agreed, I'll start identifying candidates even before we formally kick that off, no reason to wait.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Sun, anything on the schedule side beyond what we've covered?

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: The one thing I'd flag is how many of today's mitigations depend on things happening in parallel rather than in sequence, the bead-blast decision, the certification decoupling, the calibration station timeline all assume Rafael's geometry lock happens on schedule and everyone else moves the moment it does.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: If there's any hidden sequential dependency we haven't surfaced, the whole plan compresses less than we think.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: That's a fair meta-risk.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Is there anything concrete you want from this group to protect against that, or is it more of a general caution?

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: Mostly a general caution for now, though I would like a very short, almost daily check-in between Rafael, Maya, and Tomas once the rib pattern decision lands, just so nobody's waiting on an email that sits for two days at a moment when two days actually matters.

segments.speaker: spk_2

segments.text: Dele, budget risk beyond what we discussed?

segments.text: A couple of the passive components on the Aegis board are sourced from regions with currency exposure we don't have on Vantage, and if exchange rates move against us before we lock pricing with our contract manufacturer, that eats margin in a way that's outside anyone's direct control in this room.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Is that something we hedge against, or just monitor?

segments.text: For a program this size, monitoring is more realistic than formal hedging, but I want it on record as a watch item, since if it moves enough it could actually affect the retail price point marketing's been assuming.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: Good to know, I'll make sure marketing's pricing assumptions have at least a little flex built in rather than being presented as fixed this early.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Appreciate the heads up either way.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Tomas, anything from you, beyond the driver layer work we already covered?

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: Test coverage gap, honestly, on the connectivity stack specifically.

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: We've got good coverage on the sensor and calibration side because that's been a focus for months, but the cloud connectivity and the factory-mode flag work we just talked about is newer, and I don't want it to be the thing that's under-tested just because it came up later in the program.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: That's fair, I'd rather we say that out loud now than assume it's covered because everything else is.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Agreed, let's make sure the three-week abstraction layer estimate explicitly accounts for connectivity test coverage, not just sensor driver coverage.

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: It does in my head, but I'll write it down explicitly in the test plan doc so it's not just in my head.

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: While I've got the floor, one more thing on the abstraction layer, we also found that the retry and backoff behavior for the connectivity stack differs slightly between how Vantage handles it today and what the new Aegis radio module actually needs, since the radio has a different power-up latency profile after waking from sleep.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Is that a big rewrite or a parameter tweak?

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: Parameter tweak mostly, the retry timing constants need to be configurable per hardware target rather than hardcoded, which we should have done from the start honestly, this is a good forcing function to fix that properly instead of hardcoding a second set of constants for Aegis and hoping nobody forgets there are now two.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Agreed, that's exactly the kind of thing that's worth doing right once rather than patching twice.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Does that affect the factory-mode flag work we discussed earlier at all?

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: No, those are independent, the factory-mode flag controls where data goes, the retry constants control how aggressively we try to send it, they interact but they're separate pieces of configuration.

segments.speaker: spk_2
segments.text: Good, just wanted to make sure we weren't tangling two different fixes together without realizing it.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Maya, last one, anything beyond the sourcing risk Rafael just raised?

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Just that the humidity extreme test cases I mentioned earlier are still thin, twenty units isn't a huge sample at the tails of the range, and if we find something in the next batch of twenty that contradicts what we're seeing now, the "tighter tolerances" story could get more nuanced before it gets simpler.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: I'd rather flag that possibility now than have it be a surprise if the number moves later.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: Appreciated, I'll keep that in mind before committing to specific claims externally.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Good, that was a genuinely useful round, thank you all.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: While we're on that, one more thing worth raising, sales training, since this is a genuinely new product line rather than an iteration on Vantage, the field sales team needs real ramp-up.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: We're planning a half-day enablement session about a month before launch, covering the product story, the accuracy improvements Maya described, and how to answer the most likely technical objections.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: I'd like Maya or Tomas to help build the technical objection-handling section, since sales reps get asked surprisingly deep questions sometimes.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Happy to help with that, I can put together a short one-pager on the calibration story that translates the technical details into something a sales rep can actually use in a conversation without oversimplifying it into something misleading.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: That would be great, that's usually the hardest part, getting something accurate that doesn't require an engineering degree to deliver confidently.

segments.text: Is there a budget line for the enablement session itself, or does that come out of the same events pool as the trade show booth?

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: Same pool, it's a smaller cost, mostly just facilitator time and materials, nothing that needs separate approval.

segments.speaker: spk_4
segments.text: Good, just tracking where things sit.

segments.text: Anything else on go-to-market before we wrap up the general discussion?

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: Just that once we have a final product name, I'll need updated firmware version strings and any user-facing text that currently says Aegis internally, so that's worth flagging to Tomas and Maya now rather than as a surprise later.

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: Good to know, I'll grep for internal naming references once we have the go-ahead, that's a mechanical change, not a big lift.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: One more thing before action items.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Actually, I've been meaning to bring this up myself, one more topic.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: I want us to explicitly carry forward a lesson from Vantage into Aegis, tied to that drift issue with Solenne a couple weeks back, something structural we should build in from day one so we're not relying on a customer noticing before we do.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: On Vantage, the failure mode was that our compensation table quietly stopped matching the actual hardware after a component substitution, and nothing detected that mismatch automatically, it took a customer complaint and then some digging on my part.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: For Aegis, I want to build in a first-boot sanity check that cross-references the sensor's reported part identifier against the loaded compensation table, and flags a mismatch immediately rather than silently drifting for months.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: That seems like it should be cheap to build if we're doing it from the start rather than retrofitting it.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Very cheap, it's maybe a day of work if it's part of the initial architecture, the reason it wasn't on Vantage is purely that nobody thought to add it years ago, not that it's technically hard.

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: I can build that alongside the abstraction layer work, it fits naturally as part of the driver initialization sequence.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: That would be great, and longer term, once cloud connectivity is live on Aegis, I'd also like aggregate drift monitoring across the fleet, essentially watching for any part or batch that's trending away from its expected calibration curve over time, so we catch a systemic issue proactively instead of waiting for individual complaints to accumulate into a pattern.

segments.speaker: spk_3
segments.text: That sounds like a genuinely good product story too, "we monitor your sensors so you don't have to," that's worth a line in the marketing materials once it exists.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Right, though I'd want it built and proven internally for a quarter or two before we make external claims about it, I don't want a repeat of promising something before it's actually reliable.

segments.speaker: spk_0

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: It would become a bigger conversation at much higher volume, but that's a good problem to have and a future one.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Let's not scope the fleet monitoring formally today.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: The sanity check though—

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Right, that one I want locked in now, not deferred, given how cheap it is and how directly it addresses something that already burned us once.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: I'll make sure it's explicitly in scope for the abstraction layer work already approved, and that Tomas and I both treat it as in scope, not a stretch goal.

segments.speaker: spk_0
segments.text: Honestly, the fact that it's this cheap and we still didn't have it on Vantage is the part that bugs me, it's the kind of gap that only ever gets found in hindsight unless someone deliberately puts a checklist item in front of it, so I'd rather over-communicate that it's locked in than assume everyone remembers a decision from a steerco meeting three months from now.

segments.speaker: spk_1
segments.text: Agreed, noting it now.

segments.speaker: local
segments.text: Great, let's move to action items then.

segments.text: Sorry, quick one before you move on, does that trademark search cover international markets too, or just domestic for now?

segments.text: Wait, go ahead, that's a fair question actually.

segments.speaker: spk_3

segments.speaker: spk_4
segments.text: Got it, thanks, that answers it.

summary_markdown:
## Key decisions

- Demo units for the March trade show will use a bead-blasted (non-anodized) aluminum finish so the show date isn't hostage to the enclosure tool lock; production units keep the anodized finish on its normal timeline. This also decouples the demo deadline from the certification-unit deadline, since certification can wait for final-geometry, properly anodized units.
- Aegis firmware will share the Vantage codebase behind a new hardware-abstraction layer (Tomas, ~3 weeks) rather than fork, based on a proof-of-concept spike that de-risked the approach; this also lets Maya's calibration statistics tooling work unmodified across both product lines.
- A first-boot sanity check (cross-referencing sensor part ID against the loaded compensation table) is now explicitly in scope for the abstraction layer, directly addressing the root cause of the Vantage/Solenne drift issue.
- A factory-mode flag will route factory-floor calibration data away from the production cloud service, closing a gap surfaced during discussion.
- Cadence: a short interim check-in in two weeks (headlined by certification testing results) rather than waiting for the full monthly steerco.

## Discussion

Sun opened the program as "yellow": on track for the March trade show, with the enclosure as the one real risk. Rafael detailed the anodized-aluminum enclosure tooling: two prototype iterations have shown thermal hot spots near the radio module; a third rib-pattern iteration is due back Thursday, with one to two more weeks needed to lock geometry. A fourth iteration would push enclosures dangerously close to the show date, prompting the bead-blast contingency decision (budget-neutral, versus a costlier dual-sourced rush tool Dele flagged as a real hit to the ~6%-over budget). Maya walked through calibration progress on the new sensor package (20 units characterized, tighter tolerances than Vantage, pending two more weeks of validation before external claims) and the shared-architecture rationale with Tomas, including a factory calibration-station timeline (~3 weeks from geometry lock) and test-coverage plans. A risk roundtable surfaced a single-source sensor supply risk (Rafael, qualifying a second source), a sequencing/parallel-dependency risk (Sun), currency exposure on Aegis-specific components (Dele), and thin connectivity-stack test coverage (Tomas). The group also discussed go-to-market readiness — sales collateral, a pending trademark search, and a sales-enablement session Maya will help build a technical one-pager for.

## Action items

Four items: Rafael finalizes the rib-pattern decision and confirms the bead-blast path with the enclosure supplier this week; Sun holds calibration numbers back from marketing for two weeks and tracks the product-name trademark search; Maya and Tomas build the shared abstraction layer (including the sanity check and factory-mode flag) within the 3-week estimate; Dele monitors the budget contingency line and flags proactively if the enclosure situation pushes toward a 10% overage requiring formal reforecast.

## Open questions

- Whether the rib pattern locks on the third iteration or needs a fourth pass, which is the single most schedule-critical decision on the program right now.
- Final trademark clearance and timing for the product name (affects firmware strings and user-facing text).
- Whether component currency exposure will materially affect the assumed retail price point.
